System-1 Orchestration for Enterprise Conversational Agents: Typed Decisions Beside the LLM on τ²-Bench Airline

Author: Sai Vamshi Atukuri (Independent Researcher, ORCID 0009-0003-3111-7148)
Date: 2026-11-24
Status: Preprint published on Zenodo on 24 November 2026: doi:10.5281/zenodo.24501211.
Full text (HTML): https://vamshibobby.github.io/papers/system1-orchestration-tau2-airline/
PDF: https://vamshibobby.github.io/papers/system1-orchestration-tau2-airline/system1-orchestration-tau2-airline.pdf
Code: https://github.com/vamshibobby/jev-tau2-harness
DOI: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24501211
Keywords: conversational agents; tool calling; τ²-Bench; decision models; LLM orchestration; latency; guardrails

Abstract

Tool-calling chat agents spend most of a customer’s wait on serial LLM calls, and many of those
calls make decisions that a small typed-decision model or plain code can make exactly. We present a
decision-model harness, which places a decision model, one that answers yes/no and multiple-choice
questions, beside the agent’s LLM rather than in front of it. For our experiments we use Jev, a
hosted decision model that answers in about half a second. One Jev call per turn decides whether the
turn needs a tool, which of the customer’s reservations it is about, whether flight statuses matter,
whether the customer confirmed a write, and the route and date of a flight search, while a
speculative model call runs; code then issues those tool calls in one batch and checks every write
against the airline policy. On τ2-Bench Airline (50 tasks × 4 trials, Gemini 2.5 Flash as the
simulated customer) we compare three agent models alone and inside the harness. Code issued 77–84%
of all tool calls and model calls per turn fell by 24–37%. pass4, the share of tasks solved on all
four tries, rose on all three models, by 10.7 points on average, and nearly doubled on the weakest
model, Gemma 4 26B A4B (0.220 to 0.420). Conversations with a policy-forbidden write fell from 43 to
10. pass1 rose on Gemma (0.465 to 0.560) and Gemini 3.8 Flash (0.810 to 0.860) and fell slightly on
Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite. Cost fell 17% and 25% on the two Gemini models. Reply latency fell at every
percentile on Flash-Lite (median −31%, p90 −44%); on Gemini 3.8 Flash, tool-using turns were 43%
faster but the slowest turns were not. On four further open models of 30–35B parameters (50 tasks ×
1 trial), the harness raised pass1 by 6–12 points on the three that started below 0.70 and made
tool-using turns 22–41% faster on all four.

Key results (numbers as reported in the paper)

- Tool calls issued by code: 0% → 76.7–84.4% (all three models)
- Model calls per customer turn: 3.01 → 1.91 (Gemini 3.8 Flash); 2.50 → 1.90 (Flash-Lite); 2.17 → 1.58 (Gemma)
- pass4: 0.740 → 0.800 (Gemini 3.8 Flash); 0.540 → 0.600 (Flash-Lite); 0.220 → 0.420 (Gemma 4 26B A4B)
- pass1: 0.810 → 0.860 (Gemini 3.8 Flash); 0.760 → 0.735 (Flash-Lite); 0.465 → 0.560 (Gemma)
- Conversations with a policy-forbidden write: 43 → 10 (5 → 0, 9 → 3, 29 → 7)
- Agent cost per conversation: $0.0388 → $0.0323 (−17%); $0.0151 → $0.0113 (−25%); $0.0062 → $0.0065
- Reply time to first token, Flash-Lite: median 4.18 → 2.87 s (−31%); p90 12.51 → 7.05 s (−44%)
- Four further open 30–35B models (50 × 1): pass1 +6 to +12 points on the three below 0.70; tool-using turns 22–41% faster on all four
  (All numbers from Tables 3–5 and the abstract of the paper. Gemini 3.8 Flash latency comes from a separate side-by-side 50 × 1 run.)

How to cite

Choosing Affordable Language Models for Serial Fiction: Instruction Following, Creative Writing, and Story Memory

Author: Sai Vamshi Atukuri (Independent Researcher, ORCID 0009-0003-3111-7148)
Date: 2026-09-26
Status: Published on Zenodo on 26 September 2026, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.22977925.
Full text (HTML): https://vamshibobby.github.io/papers/affordable-models-for-serial-fiction/
PDF: https://vamshibobby.github.io/papers/affordable-models-for-serial-fiction/affordable-models-for-serial-fiction.pdf
Code: https://github.com/vamshibobby/webnovel-harness
DOI: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22977925
Keywords: LLM creative writing; serial fiction; instruction following; story bible; long-context memory; model selection; affordable language models; AI-assisted writing

Abstract

Our goal is to identify an affordable set of language models and prompting practices that can help a
broad community of authors begin and sustain AI-assisted serial fiction. We compare six models
priced below one US dollar per million input and output tokens through 687 chapter-generation
attempts, covering instruction detail, output constraints, reasoning settings, story bibles,
retrieval, history compression and sequential continuation. A selected novel provides a common
reference. We distinguish following the author’s brief from resembling the reference and from
writing an engaging scene. In a 144-attempt instruction-design comparison, 108 drafts were usable,
but only 44 also met the length requirement. Reference-event coverage increased from 4.7% with vague
direction to 90.7% with detailed prose instructions; numbering the same instructions yielded 88.9%
and no consistent advantage across scenes. DeepSeek V3.2 led the selected detailed-instruction
checks, GLM 5.3 Flash was the most balanced creative-scene candidate in exploratory AI readings, and
Tencent Hy3 was the most reliable writer in that comparison. Story-bible updates introduced
different risks, including retained contradictions and unexecuted repairs. The findings support
choosing models by role, specifying causal requirements and creative freedom separately, and
validating both chapters and memory updates. They are practical starting points from a single-novel
study, not a universal literary ranking.

Key results (numbers as reported in the paper)

- Writing attempts in the study: 687 across five experiment groups
- Instruction-design test: usable drafts / also met length: 108 of 144 usable; 44 met the 1,233–1,667-word band
- Original events supported, by brief: Vague 4.7%; concise 32.7%; detailed prose 90.7%; numbered 88.9%
- Numbering the same instructions (paired, scenes A/B/C): −4.2, −4.8 and +3.7 percentage points: no consistent advantage
- Full-brief requirements supported (detailed + numbered): DS3.2 97.0% (12 of 12 usable); Hy3 93.3% (12 of 12 usable)
- Hy3 with reasoning disabled vs a 1,024-token reasoning hint: Usable 2/8 → 8/8; met length 0/8 → 6/8; median time about 80 → 18 s
- Exact output constraints, all six rules together: 1 of 36 stress-test attempts (a DS4 draft)
- Summary-heavy vs full history (50 prior chapters), cost per usable chapter: −80% Gemini Lite; −56% GLM; −71% DS3.2
  (Numbers from the abstract, Tables 2, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9 and 15, and Section 3.3. Literary judgments in the paper are exploratory AI readings, not a human reader panel.)

How to cite

Atukuri, S. V. (2026). Choosing Affordable Language Models for Serial Fiction: Instruction Following, Creative Writing, and Story Memory. Zenodo. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22977925

Decisions Without Generation: What Universal Decision Models Changed About Classification, and Where a Fine-Tuned 4B Model Still Wins

Author: Sai Vamshi Atukuri (Independent Researcher, ORCID 0009-0003-3111-7148)
Date: 2026-11-27
Status: Preprint published on Zenodo on 27 November 2026: doi:10.5281/zenodo.24601222.
Full text (HTML): https://vamshibobby.github.io/papers/decisions-without-generation/
PDF: https://vamshibobby.github.io/papers/decisions-without-generation/decisions-without-generation.pdf
Code: https://github.com/vamshibobby/decisions-without-generation
DOI: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24601222
Keywords: text classification; decision models; calibration; LoRA; AI agents; tool selection; LLM serving cost; selective prediction

Abstract

The release of TypeSafe’s Jev, a hosted “System One” model that answers typed questions about a
piece of text with calibrated probabilities in a single non-autoregressive pass, did something that
a decade of text classifiers had not: it put a classifier into the hands of people who never trained
one, and it was pointed at decisions where nobody had thought to use a classifier before. Browser
agents ask it which element to click. Orchestrators ask it which tool to call and whether the call
is risky. Harnesses ask it whether a trajectory succeeded or is looping. Moderation pipelines ask it
whether a response is harmful. We treat these as new problem statements and ask a practical
question: on the decision surfaces Jev made visible, how do the classical tools of the field,
sentence-embedding classifiers, zero-shot log-probability readouts, and classifier heads on a small
fine-tuned language model, perform in accuracy, calibration, latency and cost? We build four designs
on Qwen3.5-4B that share Jev’s interface (state plus one to five typed questions, one forward pass,
one probability vector per question): a zero-shot logprob readout, LoRA with linear heads, LoRA with
a per-option [CLS] scorer for dynamic option sets, and a LoRA language model read at answer slots.
We evaluate them, an embedding floor, and Jev on sixteen datasets spanning intent routing,
moderation, tool selection, browser-step selection, agent-trajectory judging, fact verification,
adversarial inference and knowledge, with temperature fitted on a disjoint calibration split and
every model measured on the same rows. The picture is consistent. With a few thousand labels and ten
to eighty minutes on a rented GPU, a fine-tuned 4B model matches or beats the universal model on
every agentic decision we measured, at 55–85 ms per decision against roughly 250 ms for the API, and
at $1–9 per million decisions on a fully used GPU against $10–144 billed per token. The head design
barely matters; training does. Jev, in turn, is the strongest zero-label decision model we measured,
beats our zero-shot 4B on every reading task, escalates when evidence is missing where our best
fine-tuned model has learned to guess, and is the most conservative scorer at high confidence. On
knowledge we ran two probes: on the public MMLU-Pro benchmark Jev leads a one-pass 4B by nineteen
points, but on ObscureWikiQA, a set built from articles too obscure for any benchmark, its closed-
book accuracy is within the confidence interval of the 4B’s, so the MMLU-Pro lead reflects that
benchmark rather than a general advantage. Decomposing a decision into typed sub-questions, the
lever its users report most often, did not help on the one task where we tested it. We also analyse
serving: a hosted API scales out by adding concurrent calls, while a self-hosted classifier is bound
by the capacity of its GPU, and we measure what continuous batching does to that ceiling on one task
(one A100 goes from 17 requests per second one at a time to 73 under load) and where the cost curves
cross. We also build Jev’s serving contract on the 4B itself, encoding the state once with the
untouched base weights and fanning isolated question segments out over the cached state: accuracy
matches or slightly exceeds the shared-prompt arms and a marginal question costs two milliseconds,
at the price of a second forward pass. We conclude that universal decision models democratised
classification, that in most labelled, high-volume settings a purpose-tuned small classifier will
still do the better job, and that both are needed. We close with a research direction: reinforcement
learning for decision models whose reward comes from the environment the decision acts in, rather
than from a loss that penalises false positives and negatives, which would reduce to supervised
training with a different name.

Key results (numbers as reported in the paper)

- Agentic decisions (fine-tuned 4B vs Jev): With a few thousand labels and ten to eighty minutes on a rented GPU, a fine-tuned 4B model matches or beats the universal model on every agentic decision measured
- Latency per decision: 55–85 ms (fine-tuned 4B) against roughly 250 ms for the API
- Cost per million decisions: $1–9 on a fully used GPU against $10–144 billed per token
- Mind2Web browser-step selection: One epoch (6,787 steps, about 20 minutes on an A100) gives 6 points over the universal model in distribution and 5 to 6 on unseen websites and domains
- Knowledge: Jev leads a one-pass 4B by nineteen points on MMLU-Pro; on ObscureWikiQA its closed-book accuracy is within the confidence interval of the 4B's
- Continuous batching, one A100: 17 requests per second one at a time → 73 under load
- Jev-style fan-out on the 4B: Accuracy matches or slightly exceeds the shared-prompt arms; a marginal question costs two milliseconds
- Decomposition into typed sub-questions: Did not help on the one task where it was tested
  (Sixteen datasets spanning intent routing, moderation, tool selection, browser-step selection, agent-trajectory judging, fact verification, adversarial inference and knowledge; numbers from the abstract and Table 4.)

How to cite

Atukuri, S. V. (2026). Decisions Without Generation: What Universal Decision Models Changed About Classification, and Where a Fine-Tuned 4B Model Still Wins. Zenodo. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24601222

BANKING77 Is Broken: Rethinking a Cornerstone Intent-Detection Benchmark for Enterprise Conversational Agents

Author: Sai Vamshi Atukuri (Independent Researcher, ORCID 0009-0003-3111-7148)
Date: 2026-11-27
Status: Preprint published on Zenodo on 27 November 2026: doi:10.5281/zenodo.24601220.
Full text (HTML): https://vamshibobby.github.io/papers/banking77-is-broken/
PDF: https://vamshibobby.github.io/papers/banking77-is-broken/banking77-is-broken.pdf
Code: https://github.com/vamshibobby/banking77-x
DOI: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24601220
Keywords: intent detection; BANKING77; benchmark audit; label noise; conversational agents; ambiguity detection; out-of-scope detection; decision models

Abstract

BANKING77 has been the default benchmark for fine-grained intent detection since 2020, and it is now
also a launch benchmark for a new class of decision models that return typed, probabilistic answers
instead of text. We show that it no longer measures what modern conversational agents need. An audit
of all 13,083 queries finds that about 1.1% of labels are clearly wrong and a further ~6% are
genuinely ambiguous, so the realistic accuracy ceiling is 96–97%, not 100%. Over half of the test
set has a near-paraphrase in the training set, and every reported improvement since 2020 sits inside
the benchmark’s ±0.85-point confidence interval. The benchmark is also blind by construction to what
enterprise assistants actually face: out-of-scope requests, underspecified requests that require a
clarifying question, messages with several requests, multi-turn context and escalation to a human.
We introduce BANKING77-X, a 20,381-record extension that keeps the 77 intents, so existing models
can be evaluated as they are, corrects the original’s audited labels, and makes these cases first-
class: every user turn receives one of 80 categories (77 intents plus ambiguous, multi_intent and
out_of_scope), along with a three-level hierarchy, escalation signals and entity spans. All new
items were generated by one large language model (Claude Opus) and kept only if a second model of
the same family (Claude Sonnet), labelling blind, agreed under strict rules; the data may therefore
favour Claude-family readings, and we exclude Claude models from the benchmark. No new item was
labelled by a human; a small human spot-check of a stratified sample (36 labels) found no errors. We
benchmark 22 systems: six commercial decision models, fourteen open models under 9B parameters run
zero-shot, and two embedding classifiers. A classifier trained on BANKING77 labels clean queries
with 0.91 accuracy but scores 0.48 on BANKING77-X; the best decision models reach 0.88; the best
open model reaches 0.77. Detecting ambiguity is the hardest part: most systems that label intents
with 90%+ accuracy almost never recognise that a message is ambiguous.

Key results (numbers as reported in the paper)

- Clearly wrong BANKING77 labels: about 1.1% (~140 rows, 95% CI 102–211), including ~36 in the test set
- Genuinely ambiguous BANKING77 queries: a further ~6%; realistic accuracy ceiling 96–97%, not 100%
- Train–test leakage: 58% of test items have a training neighbour at cosine ≥0.90 (28.6% at ≥0.95)
- Statistical resolution of the test set: 95% Wilson interval about ±0.85 points near 94% accuracy; no full-data improvement since 2020 clearly clears it
- BANKING77-X size: 20,381 records (12,654 train / 1,735 dev / 5,992 test), 80 categories
- Classifier trained on BANKING77 only: 0.91 category accuracy on clean queries, 0.476 BANKING77-X score
- Best decision models (BANKING77-X score): Perplexity Decider 27B 0.877; Jev 1.13 0.869; Mercury Decide 0.829
- Best open models under 9B, zero-shot: Gemma 4 E4B 0.766; Qwen3.5-4B 0.749
  (Scores are on test-mini (931 chat records); see Table 4. Total API cost of the benchmark was about $1.84.)

How to cite

Atukuri, S. V. (2026). BANKING77 Is Broken: Rethinking a Cornerstone Intent-Detection Benchmark for Enterprise Conversational Agents. Zenodo. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24601220
